turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I'd like help putting Shōkai on my store. I run Northline Supply on WordPress — ceramic desk planters. I'm Alex Rivera, I own it.

turns.name: Muse
turns.text:
I can help design your welcome, visitor rules and example visits here. Keeping the shop available between chats needs a separate connected service, and that part isn't connected yet. Would planning be useful?

Before we go further: Northline Supply is on WordPress, not Shopify or WooCommerce. The first-release route is Shopify first, with WooCommerce as the sibling chapter. I don't yet have a tested path for WordPress/other platforms. 

That said, we can still plan your welcome, draft visitor rules and rehearse the experience here. When it's time to connect a live door, you'd need a technical helper to set up the WordPress side—or we could explore whether WooCommerce might work for you instead.

Does planning-only make sense for now, or would you rather wait until a WordPress path is ready?

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Yeah, planning makes sense. I'd rather get ahead of it anyway—understand how this thing works before we're live. And honestly, WooCommerce might be worth looking at down the road if WordPress gets messy. Let's start with the welcome and rules. What do you need from me?

turns.name: Muse
turns.text:
Great. Let me start by understanding your place.

**First: your public storefront.** I'd like to look at what shoppers see—your homepage, product pages, about section, policies. That'll help me draft a welcome that sounds like Northline Supply, not generic. Do I have permission to browse your site, or would you rather paste some key pages?

**Second: your voice.** When you say "ceramic desk planters"—is that the whole catalog, or do you carry other things? What's the tone you want visitors to feel? (Quiet and thoughtful? Energetic? Professional? Something else?)

**Third: who approves this.** Before anything goes live, we'll need to confirm you control the store. For now, I'm just noting: you're Alex Rivera, owner. Anything else I should know about who can sign off?

Start with whichever feels easiest. I'll ask one thing at a time.

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text: How does that work? You can get technical if you need to — I want to understand the mechanism.

turns.name: Muse
turns.text:
Good question. Here's the plain version first, then the technical detail.

**Plain version:** I can read public web pages the same way you do—open your site, look at product descriptions, photos, policies, whatever shoppers see. I use that to understand your place and draft a welcome that fits. I'm not logging into your WordPress admin or changing anything. Just reading what's public.

**Technical detail, since you asked:** I have access to web browsing tools—I can fetch and parse HTML, follow links, extract text and structured data. It's similar to how a search engine crawler works. I send an HTTPS request to your domain, get back the page, and read it. No authentication, no admin access, no mutations. If your site blocks automated requests or requires login to see product pages, the fallback is you paste the public content here and I work from that instead.

For the planning phase, that's all I need. Later, when a live door connects to your store—whether WordPress or WooCommerce—that's a different integration. The door would need authorized API access to read your catalog (prices, inventory, product details) and potentially create draft orders if you want that. That's a separate conversation with different permissions and safeguards. Today I'm just reading what your customers already see.

Does that make sense? Ready to share your store URL, or would you rather describe it?

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text: That makes sense. Yeah, go ahead and browse the site—northlinesupply.com. Poke around, see what we've got. I'm curious what you'll pick up on. Fair warning though: it's pretty minimal right now. That's kind of intentional. We keep it clean.

turns.name: Muse
turns.text:
I'll take a look at northlinesupply.com and come back with what I find. Give me a moment.

I'm unable to open that page from here. I can't reach northlinesupply.com—either the site isn't publicly accessible right now, or there's a network limitation on my end.

Here's what we do: could you paste a few key sections? Homepage text, a product description or two, your about/mission statement if you have one, and any shipping or return info. Even a rough copy-paste is fine. That'll give me enough to understand the clean, minimal feel you're going for and draft something that fits.

Or if you'd rather describe it—what the homepage says, what a typical planter listing looks like, the vibe—I can work from that too.

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text:
No problem. Let me grab some of that for you.

**Homepage:** "Northline Supply. Ceramic desk planters for focused work. Handmade, minimal design. Ships within 5 days."

**Sample product:** "Matte white cylinder planter, 4-inch. Drainage hole. $28. Pairs well with small succulents or air plants."

**About:** "We make ceramic planters that don't distract. Clean lines, natural materials. Each piece is thrown and finished by hand in Portland, Oregon."

**Shipping:** "Orders ship USPS Priority within 5 business days. $6 flat rate. Free shipping over $50."

**Returns:** "30 days, full refund if unused. Damaged pieces replaced at no cost."

That's the gist.

turns.name: Muse
turns.text:
Perfect. I've got a clear picture now.

**What I'm seeing:** Northline Supply is handmade ceramic planters—minimal, focused aesthetic. Portland-based, intentional craftsmanship. Price point around $28 per piece, clean product language. The whole vibe is "doesn't distract," which tells me your customers are people who care about their workspace, not impulse buyers. Shipping is straightforward and honest.

**Your voice:** Calm, direct, no fluff. "Focused work" and "doesn't distract" are doing a lot of work. That's your north star for the welcome.

Before I draft it, a few quick questions:

1. **What's the main thing you want a visitor to do?** Browse your catalog and maybe suggest an order for you to consider? (Nothing would be created in your store—just a practice suggestion.) Or something else?

2. **Any questions you'd want to ask visitors upfront?** Like, "What's your workspace like?" or "Do you have a preference for size?" Or keep it completely open?

3. **Anything that should stay private?** Back-office stuff, other customers' orders, pricing strategy—anything you don't want a visiting assistant to see or know about?
